story: After Disco Demolition Night in Chicago, dance music passed from major labels to DJs in the city's underground clubs. Frankie Knuckles, who had moved from New York City, was resident DJ at the Warehouse in Chicago from 1977 to 1982, where the dancers were mainly black gay men. Ron Hardy played at its successor, the Music Box, from 1983. Knuckles mixed songs together instead of playing records one after another, and added a drum machine and a reel-to-reel tape player to make new tracks. By one account, the Importes Etc. record shop labelled his records "As Heard at the Warehouse", shortened to "House". In 1984 Jesse Saunders made "On and On" with a Roland TR-808 drum machine and a TB-303 bass synthesizer. From 1985 more Chicago DJs released their own tracks on newly affordable electronic instruments, for clubs serving mainly black, Mexican American and gay audiences. Phuture's "Acid Tracks" (1987) started acid house. In January 1987 Steve "Silk" Hurley's "Jack Your Body" reached number one in the UK, and Britain had its Second Summer of Love in 1988 and 1989.

story: Detroit's high-school parties of the early 1980s danced to European disco, which locals called "progressive", and to synth-pop. The radio shows of The Electrifying Mojo played Kraftwerk and Yellow Magic Orchestra next to disco and funk. Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson met at Belleville High School, about 30 miles from Detroit, where they were among the few black students. Atkins took the word techno from Alvin Toffler's "techno rebels" when his duo Cybotron, with Richard Davis, released "Alleys of Your Mind" in 1981. The three went to Chicago to hear Ron Hardy and Frankie Knuckles, and joined that dance music to the mechanical sound of Kraftwerk, reflecting post-industrial Detroit. Rejecting the formulas of Motown and R&B, they called their music "post-soul". In 1985 Atkins founded the Metroplex label and released Model 500's "No UFO's"; May's "Strings of Life" followed in 1987. In 1988 the British compilation Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit, compiled by Neil Rushton and May, set techno apart from Chicago house. In the early 1990s clubs such as Tresor opened in empty buildings in former East Berlin, and by 1999 the Love Parade drew a reported 1.5 million people.

story: Dancehall began in the late 1970s among working-class people in inner-city Kingston who could not go to dances uptown. As Edward Seaga's government replaced Michael Manley's, music moved away from internationally oriented roots reggae toward local listeners. Radio would not play it, so it spread through sound systems and record dealers. Deejays toasted over rhythm tracks from 1960s and 1970s reggae. Sound systems such as Killimanjaro and Black Scorpio brought new deejays such as General Echo and Yellowman, whose sexually explicit lyrics were called "slackness". Deejay records now mattered more than records by singers. In 1984 Wayne Smith and Noel Davey built a riddim on the "rock" preset of a Casiotone MT-40 keyboard, because Davey could not afford a Yamaha DX-7. King Jammy released it as "Under Mi Sleng Teng" in 1985, and many artists recorded over the same riddim. Afterwards most riddims were made by keyboard players alone. Shabba Ranks won a Grammy for his 1991 album As Raw as Ever, and dancehall's faster electronic beat shaped Reggae en Español.

story: Jungle grew from the British rave scene and Jamaican sound-system culture as breakbeat hardcore split apart in 1992 and 1993. Shut Up and Dance had put reggae samples into hardcore since 1990. Paul Ibiza of Ibiza Records fused bleeps and breaks with reggae basslines, and Lennie De Ice's "We Are I.E." laid a ragga bassline under the beat. DJs such as DJ Ron, DJ Hype and Fabio & Grooverider played it at clubs such as AWOL and Roast, and on pirate stations such as Kool FM. One account says the name came from a chant, "all the junglists", that Rebel MC sampled in 1991 from a Jamaican sound-system tape. Cheaper sampling let young people make tracks at home, and many producers sampled the "Amen break". It drew black British youths more than other rave styles did. In 1994 and 1995 M-Beat and General Levy's "Incredible" reached the UK top 40, Kiss 100 started a jungle show and BBC Radio 1 followed with One in the Jungle. Dillinja, Roni Size and Krust then moved the sound toward drum and bass, and Roni Size and Reprazent's New Forms won the Mercury Music Prize in 1997.

story: Until the late 1980s, Japanese popular song was sold as kayōkyoku, a name in use since the 1920s. When the singer Hibari Misora died in 1989, many kayōkyoku television shows, among them The Best Ten, were closed. The new name came from J-Wave, a radio station in Roppongi that opened on 1 October 1988 and at first played no Japanese music. Around the turn of 1989 its managing director Hideo Saitō and record-company staff planned to play Japanese records there and chose a "J" to label them. At first the word covered Western-style acts such as Pizzicato Five and Flipper's Guitar. From about 1990 to 1993 the charts were led by acts from the Being agency, among them B'z and Tube, whose songs were sold through tie-ins. From 1994 to 1997 the producer Tetsuya Komuro led dance and techno acts such as TRF and Namie Amuro, with 20 songs that each sold over a million copies. Japan's physical music sales peaked in 1998, and Hikaru Utada's first Japanese album, First Love, released in March 1999, became the best-selling album in Oricon history. In December 2002 the phone company au opened a market for ringtone song downloads.

story: After the Korean War (1950–1953), Korean singers earned money playing country, blues, jazz and rock and roll for US troops who stayed. The 1980s belonged to ballad singers such as Lee Moon-se and Byun Jin-sub. On 11 April 1992 the trio Seo Taiji and Boys debuted on an MBC talent show with "I Know" and got the jury's lowest rating, but the song and their first album became hits. The song's new jack swing beat and lyrics about the problems of Korean society were followed by hip-hop and R&B acts such as Deux, 1TYM and Drunken Tiger. Their teenage following turned the industry towards teen pop, and in 1995 producer Lee Soo-man, educated in the US, founded SM Entertainment. Agencies took the idol business model of J-pop. Lee's boy band H.O.T. debuted in 1996 after training in singing, dancing, etiquette and handling the media; "Candy" set a formula of energetic dance steps later idol groups adopted. After the 1997 Asian financial crisis H.O.T. released a Mandarin-language album, and the government funded a K-pop department. By the early 2000s TVXQ and BoA succeeded in Japan, and in 2019 South Korea ranked sixth among music markets, led by BTS and Blackpink.

story: In 1986 ten Swedish disc jockeys, among them Dag Krister Volle, known as Denniz PoP, founded the remix service SweMix. In 1992 Denniz PoP remade a demo by Ace of Base as "All That She Wants". Denniz took on Karl Martin Sandberg, singer of the funk metal band It's Alive, as a songwriter and renamed him Max Martin. From 1996 Cheiron wrote and produced in a joint venture with Zomba, starting with the Backstreet Boys' debut album. Early in 1998 Jive Records sent the 16-year-old Britney Spears to record "...Baby One More Time", a song first written for TLC, who had turned it down. Denniz PoP died of cancer on 30 August 1998, aged 35, and Cheiron closed in 2000. story: Reggaeton grew out of Panama's Spanish-language reggae of the late 1980s; reggae had reached Panama with Jamaican and Barbadian workers who built the Panama Canal. Its drum pattern was first featured in Shabba Ranks's "Dem Bow" of 1991, and the producers Steely & Clevie are credited with creating it. From 1992 DJ Playero and rappers from around San Juan and Carolina, Puerto Rico, recorded in carports and housing projects such as Villa Kennedy. Their cassettes were sold from car trunks; Daddy Yankee is credited with first saying "reggaeton" on Playero 34. In February 1995 police raided six San Juan record stores and seized hundreds of cassettes under obscenity laws; schools banned baggy clothing and underground music. That year DJ Negro put out The Noise 3 with a label reading "Non-explicit lyrics", and it was a hit. In 2004 reggaeton spread through the United States and Europe, and Daddy Yankee's album Barrio Fino and its single "Gasolina" opened the door for it worldwide. In 2017 the video for "Despacito" by Luis Fonsi featuring Daddy Yankee reached one billion views in less than three months. From 2018, starting with "Te Boté", producers turned to a sharper, minimalist dembow.

That year Fuse ODG travelled to Ghana, found the Azonto dance, and back in London mixed it with UK funky and grime. D'banj's "Oliver Twist" reached number 9 on the UK Singles Chart in 2012. In 2013 Davido put an instructional dance video for "Skelewu" on YouTube and asked fans to upload their own. In 2014 afroswing grew out of it in the UK, popularised by J Hus. story: Kanye West had used Auto-Tune on background vocals for The College Dropout in 2004, but not for lead vocals. In 2008, working on remixes of Lil Wayne's "Lollipop" and Young Jeezy's "Put On", he took to it, and T-Pain coached him. After his mother Donda died in November 2007 and his engagement to Alexis Phifer ended in April 2008, West recorded 808s & Heartbreak in September and October 2008 in Burbank, California and Honolulu. He flew in Kid Cudi, whose 2008 mixtape A Kid Named Cudi he admired, and Cudi co-wrote four songs. story: Amapiano mixes kwaito, deep house, gqom, jazz, soul and lounge music. In the 2000s DJ Spoko, who had moved to Atteridgeville west of Pretoria, DJ Mujava and others made bacardi house, known as sgubhu saPitori. Because amapiano resembles bacardi house, some place its start in Pretoria, but accounts from the Johannesburg townships differ and no single founder is agreed. Kabelo Motha, known as Kabza de Small, moved from eMalahleni to Pretoria and began his music career in 2009. His single "Umshove" came out in 2018, and on 1 October 2019 he released the EP Piano Hub with DJ Maphorisa. The name is the Zulu word for "pianos", and the music is built on piano melodies and log-drum basslines. Kabza de Small credits the producer MDU aka TRP with finding the log-drum sound while trying out new plug-ins. Young people posted dance videos set to it on social media, which fed the dance scene in South Africa. In 2019 it spread across Africa, and in 2022 the online store Beatport gave it its own charts. In 2023 Tyla's "Water" became the first song by a South African soloist to enter the US Billboard Hot 100 in 55 years.

story: Latin trap descends from southern hip hop and trap, influenced by reggaeton, R&B and urbano music. Ozuna dates it to "El Pistolón" in 2007, by Arcángel & De la Ghetto, Yaga & Mackie and Jowell & Randy in Puerto Rico; De la Ghetto says he began around 2005 or 2006. Its reggaeton artists wanted to bring American hip hop and R&B to a Spanish-speaking audience. Around 2014 Alvaro Diaz, Myke Towers and Fuete Billete posted songs on social media, and in 2015 and 2016 Noriel, Anuel AA, Bryant Myers and others put trap songs on SoundCloud. In July 2017 The Fader wrote that Puerto Rican rappers had taken trap's lurching bass lines and jittering 808s. They rapped and sang through autotune, in Spanish or Spanglish, about street life, violence, sex and drugs. Jorge Fonseca's compilation Trap Capos: Season 1 was the first Latin trap LP to top Billboard's Latin Rhythm Albums. In 2018 Cardi B's "I Like It", with Bad Bunny and J Balvin, became the first Latin trap song to reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100. In Argentina, Duki, YSY A, Cazzu and others carried it across South America, faster than in Puerto Rico.

story: Trap is named after the Atlanta term "trap house", a drug house, and the Atlanta rapper T.I. says he coined the word with his 2003 album Trap Muzik. In the mid-2000s Atlanta producers DJ Toomp, Shawty Redd and Zaytoven set its sound: synth, orchestra and string swells over 808 kick drums. Lex Luger, born in 1991, drummed in church bands, made beats on an unlicensed copy of FL Studio and from late 2008 posted them on Myspace. In 2009 the rapper Waka Flocka Flame wrote back, and later flew him to Atlanta. Luger produced most of Waka's album Flockaveli (5 October 2010): 808 trills, bass kicks, hand claps, dense synthesizers and shifting sub-bass layers under constant ad-libs. He produced more than 200 songs in 2010 and 2011, and other producers copied his sounds. Beats often run in half-time, around 70 BPM, for finer hi-hat subdivisions. The trio Migos, formed in Lawrenceville, Georgia, in 2008, broke out in 2013 with "Versace", produced by Zaytoven. In Chicago, Chief Keef's "I Don't Like" and "Love Sosa" spawned drill as a subgenre of trap. Katy Perry's "Dark Horse" with Juicy J reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 2014.

story: David Guetta, born and raised in Paris, began as a DJ in Parisian nightclubs and discovered house music on French radio in 1987. Axwell, Steve Angello and Sebastian Ingrosso formed Swedish House Mafia in late 2008 and, with Avicii, took progressive house into the mainstream. From 2009 Guetta scored crossover hits with pop and hip-hop singers: Kelly Rowland on "When Love Takes Over", the Black Eyed Peas on "I Gotta Feeling", Sia on "Titanium". Tim Bergling, born in Stockholm in 1989, taught himself on a pirated copy of FL Studio, and as Avicii had his first Billboard Hot 100 entry with "Levels" in 2011. In the late 2000s the American music industry took up the term EDM to re-brand US rave culture. Mixmag called the result a "drop-heavy, stadium-filling" main stage sound. Avicii and Swedish House Mafia played arenas rather than clubs; in December 2011 Swedish House Mafia became the first electronic act to sell out Madison Square Garden. Avicii's 2013 "Wake Me Up", sung by soul singer Aloe Blacc, drew on bluegrass. The American EDM market began to wane in 2016, and in April that year Guetta and Showtek released a single called "The Death of EDM".
